1.pericope_label: Come near, ye nations, to hear; and hearken, ye people: let the earth hear, and all that is therein; the world, and all things that come forth of it. For the indignation of the LORD is upon all nations, and his fury upon all their armies: he hath utterly destroyed them, he hath delivered them to the slaughter. Their slain also shall be cast out, and their stink shall come up out of their carcases
debates: How far the prophecy reaches: Clarke holds the images cannot be confined to any calamity yet suffered and makes Edom a type of the last adversary, with the prophecy still to be accomplished; Ellicott sets the chapter in a definite reign with the Assyrian attack in the background and reads Edom as a representative instance; Keil and Delitzsch call it an apocalyptic finale carrying us away from the stage of history.

Who is being summoned: Gill clears away a reading that makes it the Jews and another that makes it a call to hear the Gospel, since bad news and not good is announced, while Calvin says the address is to the Gentiles but the prophet has his eye principally on the Church.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report that the different impression these chapters make has raised doubts about their authenticity, and answer that the relation later prophets stand in to them is enough to drive the doubts away.
Calvin notices that the prophet speaks of future events in the past tense, to set them immediately before the eyes of people lying low under adversity.
Henry says the inanimate products of the earth are summoned as more likely to hearken than sinners, whose hearts are hardened against the calls of God.

4.pericope_label: And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll ... For my sword shall be bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my curse, to judgment. The sword of the LORD is filled with blood ... for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea
debates: Why the sword is bathed in heaven: Clarke calls the received reading improper, since the sword was only prepared for slaughter there, rejects one proposed emendation as premature, and follows the sense of an old version without knowing its reading; Ellicott suggests the dipping by which steel was tempered; Calvin answers instead from the secret decree, by which the sword is already bloody in God’s sight while the wicked are untouched.
outliers: Calvin insists the dissolving of the heavens relates to men’s apprehension, since heaven is not moved out of its place, and that men who fear no God are justly left to tremble at the rustling of a falling leaf.
Wesley states a rule of reading, that prophetic writers describe great calamities in words belonging to the day of judgment and deliverances in words belonging to the resurrection.

Calvin does not pretend the sacrifice is a comfortable figure, granting that the taking of life, the reeking blood and the stench of the smoke might repel a spectator, and that this slaughter too was hideous to behold.
Clarke traces a line of dependence from this passage to a later prophet who imitated it, and from that prophet to a later vision still.
themes: A sword prepared before it falls

7.pericope_label: And the unicorns shall come down with them, and the bullocks with the bulls; and their land shall be soaked with blood ... For it is the day of the LORD’s vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion. And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch ... It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever
debates: What animal is named in the seventh verse: Gill offers the rhinoceros or the buffalo and denies there is any such creature as the unicorn, Clarke reports wild goats and prefers the rhinoceros, Ellicott prefers the aurochs and lists the buffalo, an antelope and a species of wild ox proposed from Assyrian inscriptions, and Wesley leaves it at a beast of great strength.

Who is recompensed in the eighth verse: Clarke re-derives the noun and renders it the year of recompense to the defender of the cause of Zion, reporting an old version that has simply the Judge of Zion.
outliers: Henry takes the burning country three ways at once and marks his own uncertainty about the third, saying the earth will, for aught he knows, be turned into a hell to those who set their affections on earthly things.

Calvin defends the hyperbole, saying the Lord is compelled to speak so because plain words would make no impression, and that the prophets treated of things generally thought incredible, so that many supposed they spoke at random.

Calvin notices what the passage does not say, that the unquenched fire cuts off all hope of pardon and the contrast must be supplied by the reader, since some mitigation is always held out to the people of God.
themes: A quarrel at last brought to judgment

11.pericope_label: But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness. They shall call the nobles thereof to the kingdom, but none shall be there ... The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow
debates: What the creatures are: Clarke names every one and gives derivations, Ellicott reports the naturalists on the first four and takes the later names into mythical zoology, identifying the screech owl with the night-demon of Jewish legend, while Calvin says twice that the commentators are not agreed and that it would serve no purpose to be uneasy about the exact meanings.

Whether the twelfth verse can be construed at all: Clarke says one word attached to it makes it inexplicable, that he knows of no tolerable explanation yet given, and moves the word to the previous verse with a letter or two supplied.
outliers: Calvin reports that some give the measuring line an opposite sense and apply it to the Jews, prefers to keep it with the Edomites, and supports himself from a later prophet whose passage he calls an approbation of this prophecy.

Ellicott observes that the kingship of Edom seems to have been elective and that no chief in the recorded list is the son of his predecessor, so that the prophecy leaves neither electors nor anyone to elect.
Calvin says palaces built so that the memory of their builders might be handed down become, when men are banished and beasts move in, monuments of foolish ambition instead of trophies of a name.
themes: A land given over to wild creatures
A plumb-line used for pulling down
Nobles with nothing left to rule

16.pericope_label: Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them. And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it unto them by line: they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein
debates: What the book of the Lord is: Gill lays out four answers, the book of the law, the book of Genesis, the book of God’s decrees and this prophecy itself, and chooses the last, with Keil and Delitzsch agreeing; Calvin calls the decree reading ingenious but not sufficiently natural and settles instead on the Law; Ellicott leaves the choice open between this section and the whole collection.
outliers: Ellicott cautions that the decay of the country was very gradual, the ruins of its chief cities being of Roman origin and indicating a period of culture and prosperity reaching far into the history of the Empire.
Gill draws a corollary from the title, that the book being called the book of the Lord shows it was written by divine inspiration.
Clarke lists manuscript variants and ends by admitting that to see their importance the Hebrew must be consulted.

Calvin infers that no one may promise himself a permanent abode except by lot and on condition of leaving it when God calls, and then turns it to comfort, that if God keeps wild beasts in their allotted possession he will much more preserve men.
themes: A prophecy left to be checked
